title: The Smartest Crow in the Village
summary: A fable about a calm, clever crow who uses her memory of the land to lead her flock to hidden water during a terrible drought.
poll: Staying calm and thinking carefully is more useful in a crisis than acting fast.

versions.title: The Smartest Crow
versions.text:
A flock of birds lived on a dry hill. One bird was a crow. She was old. She was wise.

One year, no rain came. It was a drought. The ponds went dry. The streams went dry, too. The flock had no water.

Most birds got scared. They flew here. They flew there. They found no water. They got tired.

But the crow did not get scared. She stayed calm. She had seen dry years before. She could remember old water spots.

She sat and thought. She remembered a spring by some rocks. She remembered a pool under a tree. She remembered water in a log.

She said, "Follow me." She led the flock to the spring. Then to the pool. Then to the log. The birds drank and drank.

At last, the rain came back. The flock was safe. The crow's calm mind had saved them all.

versions.title: The Smartest Crow
versions.text:
A flock of birds lived together on a dry hill. One of the birds was a crow. She was old and wise, and she had lived there a long time.

One year, no rain fell at all. It was a hard drought. The ponds dried up. The streams dried up, too. The flock had no water to drink.

Most of the birds got scared. They flew here and there. They could not find water, and they grew tired and sad.

But one crow did not get scared. She stayed calm. She had lived through dry years before, and she could remember water in other spots.

She sat and thought hard. She remembered a spring behind some rocks. She remembered a pool under a big tree. She remembered water inside an old log, too.

The crow called out, "Follow me!" She led the flock to the spring first. Then she led them to the pool. Then she led them to the log. The birds drank and drank.

At last, the rain came back. The flock was safe and happy. The crow's calm mind had saved them all.

A flock of birds lived on a dry hillside near a village. One bird was a crow. She was old and wise. She had lived there longer than any other bird.

One year, a drought struck the land. Rain did not fall for many weeks. The ponds dried up completely. The streams dried up, too. Soon the flock had no water nearby.

Most of the birds became scared. They flew here and there. They searched all around, but found no water. They grew tired, thirsty, and sad.

One crow, however, did not get scared. She stayed calm instead. She had lived through dry years before. She could remember water hiding in other spots.

She sat quietly and thought hard. She remembered a spring behind some rocks. She remembered a pool under a big fig tree. She remembered water inside an old hollow log.

The crow called to the flock, "Follow me, and do not be afraid." She led them to the spring first. Then she led them to the pool. Then she led them to the log. The birds drank deeply at each stop.

At last, the rain came back. It filled the ponds again. The flock was safe and happy. They all learned one thing: the crow's calm mind had saved them all.

versions.title: The Smartest Crow in the Village
versions.text:
A flock of birds lived on a dry, rocky hillside near a quiet village. One bird was an old, wise crow. She had lived there far longer than any other bird in the flock.

One year, a harsh drought struck the land. Week after week passed without a drop of rain. The ponds dried up completely. The streams dried up, too. Soon the flock had no water anywhere nearby.

Most of the birds became scared and confused. They flew here and there, searching in every direction. But they could not find any water at all. They grew tired, thirsty, and sad.

One crow, however, refused to get scared. She stayed calm instead, trusting what she knew. She had lived through dry years before. She could remember water hiding in spots the younger birds had forgotten.

She sat quietly and thought hard, picturing the land she had watched for many seasons. She remembered a spring hidden behind some rocks. She remembered a pool shaded by a fig tree. She remembered water resting safely inside an old hollow log.

The crow called out to the flock, "Follow me calmly, and do not be afraid." She led them to the spring first, then to the shaded pool, and finally to the log. The birds drank deeply at every stop along the way.

At last, the rain came back and filled the ponds once again. The flock was safe and happy. They all learned one clear lesson: the crow's calm mind and good memory had saved them all.

versions.title: The Smartest Crow in the Village
versions.text:

One year, a severe drought struck the land. Week after week passed without a drop of rain. The ground grew harder and drier each day. The ponds dried up completely, the streams vanished, and soon the flock had no water nearby.

Most of the birds reacted with panic. They flew here and there with no plan, searching wildly in every direction. But their searching found nothing. They grew exhausted, thirsty, and desperate as the drought went on.

One crow, however, refused to let panic take over. She stayed calm instead. She had lived through earlier dry years, so she could locate water that the younger birds had forgotten.

She found a quiet branch and thought hard, picturing the land she had watched for so long. She remembered a spring hidden behind some rocks. She remembered a pool shaded by an old fig tree. She remembered water resting inside a hollow log near the farm.

She used a simple, reliable method: check the nearest source first, then move to the next one. The crow called out, "Follow me calmly. Trust that I know where to go."

She led them first to the spring, then to the pool, and finally to the log. The thirsty birds drank deeply at each stop. The drought went on for many more weeks, yet the flock stayed safe because the crow kept guiding them.

At last, the rain returned and filled the ponds again. The flock was overjoyed. Every bird learned a lesson it never forgot: the crow's calm mind and reliable memory had saved the whole flock.

One year, a severe drought struck the land without warning, and conditions grew worse with each passing week. The ponds dried up completely, the streams vanished, and soon the flock had no reliable water nearby, no matter how far the younger birds searched.

She stayed calm instead, trusting the memory she had built over many seasons of careful watching. Because she had lived through earlier dry years, she knew exactly how to locate water that the younger, more anxious birds had already forgotten.

Most of the birds reacted to this crisis with panic and disorganized confusion, which only worsened their already precarious situation further. They flew here and there without any coherent plan, searching wildly in every direction, but their frantic, scattered searching turned up nothing useful, no matter how much energy they spent. The crow finally called out to the frightened flock, "Follow me calmly, and trust that my memory will guide us, step by step, until every one of us is safe."

They flew here and there without any coherent plan whatsoever, searching wildly in every direction, but their frantic, scattered searching turned up nothing useful, no matter how much energy they spent chasing false hopes. versions.text:

Most of the birds reacted to this unfolding crisis with panic and disorganized confusion that only worsened their already precarious situation, flying here and there without any coherent plan, searching wildly in every direction at once, and growing exhausted, thirsty, and increasingly desperate as the prolonged drought dragged on, steadily draining both their physical strength and their emotional resolve in equal measure.

She relied on a simple, reliable method, one refined through long experience rather than any sudden flash of inspiration: check the nearest hidden source first, then move steadily toward the next one, never doubling back without a genuinely sound reason, and she finally called out to the frightened, exhausted flock, "Follow me calmly, and trust that my memory will guide us, step by step, until every single one of us is safe." She led them first to the spring, then to the pool, and finally to the hollow log, letting the thirsty, increasingly resourceful birds drink deeply and gratefully at each stop along the carefully planned route, and although the drought dragged on for many more difficult weeks, the flock remained safe throughout because the crow kept guiding them with unwavering patience, one hidden source after another, never once losing her composure or her clear sense of direction, even as a few skeptical birds occasionally questioned her deliberately unhurried methods.

At last, the rain returned and filled the ponds once again, soaking the parched hillside until it slowly turned green with fresh new growth, and the flock was overjoyed beyond measure. Every bird understood a lesson it never forgot for the remainder of its life: the crow's calm instinct and methodical memory, cultivated patiently over years that nobody else had thought worth valuing, had saved the whole flock from a crisis that panic alone would never have managed to resolve, a truth the flock would retell to their own young for generations afterward whenever a new dry season threatened to return and test them once again.

questions.stem: What is this story mostly about?
options: A noisy flock that argues about a new hill
A calm crow who remembers water and saves her flock
A crow that teaches young birds how to sing loudly
A farmer who digs a brand new well for his animals
questions.why: The story follows a crow who stays calm during a drought and uses her memory to lead the flock to water.

wrong.A: The flock does not move to a new hill in the story.
wrong.C: The story is not about singing.
wrong.D: There is no farmer digging a well in the story.

A hungry fox hunts the birds
A drought leaves them with no water
Too much rain floods their hillside

The rain stops completely
The crow forgets where the spring is
questions.why: Because the crow stays calm and uses her memory, she is able to guide the flock safely through the drought until the rain returns.

wrong.B: The flock stays on the hillside the whole story.
wrong.C: The rain returns at the end of the story.
wrong.D: The crow remembers the spring clearly; she does not forget it.

questions.stem: Why does the author describe the panicked birds before describing the calm crow?
options: To teach readers how birds build nests in trees and bushes
To make the crow's calm thinking stand out by contrast
To explain what the weather is like in winter in the desert
To show how fast young birds can fly when they are afraid
questions.why: Showing the panicked, unsuccessful birds first makes the crow's calm, careful thinking seem even smarter by comparison.

wrong.A: The story does not explain nest building.
wrong.C: The drought happens in a dry season, and winter is not discussed.
wrong.D: Flying speed is not the point of the comparison.

LOW.prompt: Do you think the crow was the smartest bird in the flock? Explain your answer using at least two details from the story.
checklist: I clearly said what I think.
I used at least two details from the story.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
LOW.modelAnswer: I think the crow was the smartest bird in the flock. While the other birds panicked and flew around with no plan, the crow stayed calm. She also remembered hidden water in a spring, a pool, and a log from earlier dry years. Her calm, clear thinking is what saved the whole flock.

keyWords.definition: sudden, strong fear that makes people act without thinking clearly
keyWords.example: There was panic in the hallway when the lights suddenly went out.

keyWords.definition: the ability to remember things, or something that is remembered
keyWords.example: Her memory of the hiking trail helped the group find the way back.

keyWords.definition: a planned, orderly way of doing something
keyWords.example: The coach taught the team a simple method for practicing free throws.

keyWords.definition: to find the exact place where something is
keyWords.example: Rescuers used a special light to locate the missing hikers at night.

keyWords.definition: able to be trusted to work correctly every time
keyWords.example: My older brother is reliable; he always keeps his promises.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the story?
options: A flock of birds moves away from a dry hillside forever, to find a green valley, and never comes back.
A calm, experienced crow relies on her memory and a reliable method to guide her flock through a drought.
A young crow learns to fly for the very first time, with help from the flock and an old fox.
A flock of birds argues about which hill to live on, and in the end, they split into two groups.
questions.why: The story centers on an experienced crow who uses memory and a reliable method to lead her panicked flock to hidden water during a drought.

wrong.A: The flock stays on the same hillside throughout the story.
wrong.C: The crow is old and experienced, not learning to fly.
wrong.D: The birds panic about water, not about which hill to live on.

questions.stem: What does the crow rely on to locate water during the drought?
options: A map drawn by the village farmers, with springs
Advice from a wiser animal she meets on the road
Her memory of water from earlier dry years
The sound of running water nearby, heard from afar
questions.why: The crow trusts the memory she built over many seasons of careful watching to locate the hidden water sources.

wrong.A: No map is mentioned in the story.
wrong.B: The crow does not meet another animal for advice.
wrong.D: The water sources are hidden, not identified by sound.

questions.stem: What three hidden water sources does the crow remember?
options: A spring, a pool, and a hollow log
A lake, a river, and a well
A puddle, a fountain, and a tank
A pond, a stream, and a ditch
questions.why: The crow remembers a spring behind some rocks, a pool shaded by a fig tree, and water resting inside a hollow log.

wrong.B: No lake, river, or well appears in the story.
wrong.C: No puddle, fountain, or tank appears in the story.
wrong.D: No pond, stream, or ditch appears in the story.

questions.stem: In the story, the word reliable describes the crow's —
options: feathers, which are unusually colorful
voice, which is louder than other birds'
method, which can be trusted to work
nest, which is built very high up
questions.why: The crow uses a simple, reliable method, meaning a method that can be trusted to work correctly.

wrong.A: The story does not describe the crow's feather color.
wrong.B: The story does not compare bird voices.
wrong.D: The crow's nest is not described in the story.

questions.stem: Why does panic make the other birds' situation worse, based on the story?
options: Panic makes the birds too tired to fly at all, so they sit on the ground
Panic makes the birds search without a plan, wasting their strength
Panic causes the drought to last even longer than it would have
Panic makes the younger birds forget how to drink from the small pool
questions.why: The panicked birds fly here and there without any plan, and their frantic searching wastes energy while finding nothing useful.

wrong.A: The birds still fly, just without direction.
wrong.C: Panic does not affect how long the drought lasts.
wrong.D: The birds know how to drink; they simply cannot find water.

questions.stem: What can you infer about why the crow finds a quiet branch away from the panicked crowd?
options: She wants to rest and ignore the problem for a while
She needs quiet to think clearly and remember carefully
She is afraid of the other birds and wants to hide from them
She is looking for food for herself and her young birds
questions.why: The crow settles down away from the noisy, panicked crowd specifically so she can think hard and picture the landscape clearly.

wrong.A: She is not ignoring the problem; she is solving it.
wrong.C: The story gives no sign that the crow fears the other birds.
wrong.D: She is searching for water for the whole flock, not food for herself.

questions.stem: Why does the crow check the nearest hidden source first?
options: Because it is a reliable method that saves time and energy
Because the nearest source always has the most water
Because the other sources are too dangerous to reach
Because the flock told her to go there first
questions.why: Her method of checking the nearest source first, then moving steadily to the next, is a reliable way to guide the exhausted flock without wasting effort.

wrong.B: The story never compares how much water each source holds.
wrong.C: None of the sources are described as dangerous.
wrong.D: The flock follows the crow's lead; they do not direct her.

questions.stem: How does the author organize the events of the story?
options: By comparing two different flocks of birds in a drought, one after the other
By describing the drought and panic first, then the crow's calm, methodical search for water
By listing facts about crows in general, such as their size and what they eat
By telling the story backward, starting with the rain's return and ending in the drought
questions.why: The story first shows the drought arriving and the flock panicking, then shows the crow calmly locating water and leading the flock to safety.

wrong.A: Only one flock appears in the story.
wrong.C: The story is a narrative, not a list of facts.
wrong.D: The story is told in order, from the drought to the rain's return.

MID.prompt: Explain how the crow's memory and method helped her flock survive the drought. Use at least two details from the story.
checklist: I explained how the crow's memory and method helped the flock.
I used at least two details from the story.
I organized my ideas in a clear order.
MID.modelAnswer: The crow's memory and method saved her flock during the drought. Because she had lived through earlier dry years, her memory held the locations of a spring, a pool, and a hollow log that other birds had forgotten. She also used a reliable method, checking the nearest hidden source first and then moving steadily to the next one. Together, her memory and her calm method kept the whole flock safe until the rain finally returned.

keyWords.definition: done in a careful, orderly, step-by-step way
keyWords.example: The firefighters made a methodical search of every room in the building.

keyWords.definition: good at finding clever, quick ways to solve problems
keyWords.example: The resourceful campers built a shelter out of fallen branches.

keyWords.definition: a natural ability to sense or do something without having to think it through
keyWords.example: Her instinct told her something was wrong before she saw any proof.

keyWords.definition: a time of great danger or difficulty that demands quick, careful action
keyWords.example: The town worked together to get through the flooding crisis.

keyWords.definition: following a fixed, orderly plan rather than acting randomly
keyWords.example: The scientist kept a systematic record of every test she ran.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the story?
options: A flock abandons its home rather than face a drought that lasts all year.
A crow competes with other birds to find water first, and wins a prize.
A calm, experienced crow's instinct and memory resolve the crisis.
A drought permanently destroys an entire flock of birds in the mountains.
questions.why: The story shows that the crow's calm instinct and systematic use of memory, not panic, are what resolve the drought crisis for the whole flock.

wrong.A: The flock stays on the same hillside throughout the drought.
wrong.B: The crow leads the flock cooperatively; there is no competition.
wrong.D: The flock survives the drought; it is not destroyed.

questions.stem: Why does the author describe the other birds' panic in such detail before focusing on the crow?
options: To suggest that panic is the smartest response to danger
To fully explain the biology of how all birds are able to fly
To criticize the flock for choosing a dry hillside to live on
To show, by contrast, that the crow's calm method works better
questions.why: By showing the other birds' frantic, unproductive panic first, the author makes the crow's calm, methodical response stand out as clearly more effective.

wrong.A: The panicked birds' searching finds nothing, showing panic is not effective.
wrong.B: The story is not about flight biology.
wrong.C: The story does not blame the flock for where they live.

questions.stem: Based on the story, what allows the crow to locate water that the younger birds cannot find?
options: A natural ability to sense water through her feet
A systematic memory of the land built over many seasons
Help from a farmer who shows her the way
A lucky guess that happens to be correct
questions.why: The crow's ability comes from a systematic memory of the landscape, built through years of patient observation, not luck or outside help.

wrong.A: The story never describes any special sensing ability in her feet.
wrong.C: No farmer assists the crow in the story.
wrong.D: Her success comes from memory and method, not luck.

questions.stem: In the story, the word resourceful most nearly describes birds who —
options: refuse to drink any water at all
fly faster than any other bird in the flock
find clever ways to handle a hard situation
forget the drought as soon as rain returns
questions.why: The thirsty, resourceful birds make the most of each hidden water source the crow finds for them, showing resourcefulness.

wrong.A: The birds are described drinking deeply at each stop.
wrong.B: Flying speed is not connected to resourcefulness in the story.
wrong.D: Forgetting the drought is not an example of resourcefulness.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about why some birds doubt the crow's unhurried methods during the crisis?
options: They secretly know a faster route to water
They do not trust crows in general
They want to replace the crow as leader
Fear makes a careful approach feel too slow
questions.why: In a frightening crisis, a calm, step-by-step approach can feel too slow to anxious birds, even though it is the approach that actually saves them.

wrong.A: No bird in the story knows a faster route than the crow.
wrong.B: The story gives no sign of general distrust toward crows.
wrong.C: No bird tries to take over leadership of the flock.

questions.stem: How does the crow's methodical approach to the crisis compare with the flock's first reaction to it?
options: Both approaches here rely equally on luck and blind chance alone
The flock panics wastefully, while the crow's method stays calm and ordered
The flock's panic actually works just as well as the crow's careful method
The crow's careful method takes far longer than the flock's wild searching
questions.why: The flock's panicked searching is scattered and finds nothing, while the crow's systematic, step-by-step method successfully leads them to water.

wrong.A: The crow's method is clearly organized, not left to luck or chance.
wrong.C: The flock's panic finds no water at all.
wrong.D: The story does not suggest the crow's method is slower overall.

questions.stem: What is the most likely reason the crow checks the nearest hidden source before moving to the next one?
options: A systematic order saves the flock's limited strength
The nearest source always contains the most water
She forgets the locations of the farther sources
The flock insists on visiting the closest place first
questions.why: Checking the nearest source first is a systematic choice that avoids wasting the flock's limited energy as the crisis continues.

wrong.B: The story never compares the amount of water at each source.
wrong.C: The crow clearly remembers all three locations in order.
wrong.D: The crow leads; the flock does not set the order.

questions.stem: What does the crow's success ultimately suggest about surviving a crisis?
options: Only the fastest fliers can survive a serious crisis
A crisis always ends the same way no matter how it is handled
Panic is the only natural response worth trusting in danger
Calm instinct and systematic memory can resolve a crisis panic cannot
questions.why: The story's outcome suggests that the crow's calm instinct and systematic use of memory, not panic or speed, are what actually resolve a crisis.

wrong.A: Flying speed never determines the outcome in the story.
wrong.B: The outcome depends directly on the crow's calm, methodical response.
wrong.C: Panic consistently fails the other birds throughout the story.

HIGH.prompt: The poll says staying calm and thinking carefully is more useful in a crisis than acting fast. Do you agree or disagree? Support your argument with evidence from the story about the crow and the flock.
checklist: I stated a clear position on the poll statement.
I supported my position with specific evidence from the story.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that staying calm and thinking carefully is more useful in a crisis than acting fast. When the drought struck, most of the flock reacted with panic, flying wildly in every direction, but their frantic searching found nothing. The crow, by contrast, stayed calm and used her systematic memory to locate a spring, a pool, and a hollow log, one hidden source at a time. Someone might argue that acting fast matters most in an emergency, but the story shows that fast, panicked action wasted the flock's strength, while the crow's calm, methodical instinct is what actually resolved the crisis.

LOW.stem: Where is the pool that the crow remembers?
options: Under a tree
By some rocks
Inside a log
On a hill
LOW.why: The text says the crow remembered a pool under a tree.

wrong.B: The spring, not the pool, is by some rocks.
wrong.C: The water in a log is a different place.
wrong.D: The hill is where the flock lives, and it is dry.

LOW.stem: In the story, the word drought means —
options: a very loud summer storm
a kind of bird that sings
a long time with no rain
a green hill with trees
LOW.why: The text says no rain came, and the ponds and streams went dry.

wrong.A: The story has no storm until the rain returns.
wrong.B: A drought is a time of dry weather, not a bird.
wrong.D: The hill is dry, not green.

LOW.stem: Why do most of the birds get tired?
options: They sing all through the night.
They fly around and find no water.
They carry heavy sticks around.
They fight over a small pond.
LOW.why: They fly here and there, find no water, and get tired.

wrong.A: Singing is not mentioned.
wrong.C: Carrying sticks is not mentioned.
wrong.D: The ponds are dry, so there is nothing to fight over.

LOW.stem: What does the crow's call, "Follow me," show?
options: She wants to take a nap.
She is lost and scared too.
She is angry at the flock.
She knows where to find water.
LOW.why: The crow remembered the water spots, so she can lead the flock to them.

wrong.A: She is busy leading the flock to water.
wrong.B: The crow stays calm and is not scared.
wrong.C: She is helping the flock, not angry at it.

MID.stem: Where is the hollow log that the crow remembers?
options: Under the old fig tree
Behind the big rocks
Near the farm
Beside the village well
MID.why: The text says the water rests inside a hollow log near the farm.

wrong.A: The pool, not the log, is shaded by the fig tree.
wrong.B: The spring, not the log, is hidden behind rocks.
wrong.D: No well is mentioned.

MID.stem: In the story, the word desperate means —
options: glad and relaxed
very upset and afraid
proud of a good job
busy with a happy task
MID.why: The birds are exhausted and thirsty and fly everywhere searching, so they are desperate.

wrong.A: The birds are thirsty and upset, not relaxed.
wrong.C: They have found nothing to be proud of.
wrong.D: They are searching in panic, not doing a happy task.

MID.stem: Why have the younger birds forgotten where the hidden water is?
options: They have lived through fewer dry years.
The crow hid the water from them.
The water was moved to another hill.
They do not like the taste of it.
MID.why: The crow knows the sources because she lived through earlier dry years, and the younger birds have lived through fewer.

wrong.B: The crow shares the water with them.
wrong.C: The text does not say the water moved.
wrong.D: Taste is not mentioned.

MID.stem: Why does the flock stay safe even when the drought lasts many more weeks?
options: The streams come back at once.
The farm gives them water.
The birds fly to another land.
The crow keeps guiding them.
MID.why: The text says the flock stayed safe because the crow kept guiding them.

wrong.A: The streams stay dry until the rain returns.
wrong.B: The farm is only where one source is.
wrong.C: The flock stays and follows the crow.

HIGH.stem: What happened to the dry hillside when the rain returned?
options: It turned into a pond.
It was covered with snow.
It became more rocky.
It slowly turned green.
HIGH.why: The text says the rain soaked the hillside until it slowly turned green.

wrong.A: The ponds filled again, but the hillside did not become a pond.
wrong.B: Snow is not mentioned.
wrong.C: The hillside was already rocky and turned green.

HIGH.stem: In the story, the word deteriorated in "conditions deteriorated" means —
options: got much worse
stayed the same
became more calm
were forgotten
HIGH.why: Each week the sky stayed empty of clouds and the drought grew harder, so things got worse.

wrong.B: Conditions changed each week.
wrong.C: The birds became more upset, not more calm.
wrong.D: The conditions were not forgotten.

HIGH.stem: Why does the author mention that water had always been scarce on the hillside?
options: To say the village is small
To explain why crows are wise
To show the danger was greater
To list the types of birds
HIGH.why: In a place with little water already, a drought is especially dangerous.

wrong.A: The detail is about water, not village size.
wrong.B: The crow's wisdom comes from her experience, not from scarce water.
wrong.D: No list of birds is given.

HIGH.stem: What effect does the long drought have on the panicked birds?
options: It teaches them to stay calm.
It drains their strength.
It makes them fly much faster.
It helps them find the spring.
HIGH.why: The text says the long drought drained their strength and their resolve.

wrong.A: The panicked birds do not become calm.
wrong.C: They grow exhausted, not faster.
wrong.D: They find nothing until the crow leads them.
